decks.title: Principles of Inheritance and Variation — Part 1: Mendel’s laws
goals: Explain why Mendel chose the garden pea and how he designed his crosses
Work out monohybrid and dihybrid crosses with Punnett squares
Use a test cross to find an unknown genotype
State the laws of dominance, segregation and independent assortment

slides.heading: Principles of Inheritance and Variation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how Gregor Mendel discovered the rules by which characters pass from parents to offspring.

nodes.label: Counting offspring in F1 and F2

visual.alt: Flow of Mendel’s method: true-breeding parents, controlled crosses, counting offspring, laws of inheritance

slides.narration: Why do children resemble their parents, yet differ from them and from each other? Inheritance is the passing of characters from parents to offspring, and variation is the difference among individuals. The first person to find clear rules for inheritance was Gregor Mendel, who crossed pea plants and, crucially, counted the results.

slides.heading: Why the garden pea?
slides.body_md: Mendel crossed garden pea plants for **seven years (1856–1863)** and published his results in 1865. He worked with **14 true-breeding varieties**, forming **seven pairs** of contrasting traits, and analysed large samples statistically.

rows: Parents give the same trait generation after generation
Easy to score, for example tall or dwarf
Self-pollinates naturally but can be crossed by hand

visual.alt: Table of features of the garden pea and why each helped Mendel

slides.narration: Mendel chose his plant well. Peas come in true-breeding varieties that keep showing the same trait after several generations of self-pollination. Each trait comes in two clearly different forms. Pea flowers normally pollinate themselves, but Mendel could remove anthers and pollinate them by hand. And each plant gives many seeds, so he could count large numbers.

slides.heading: The seven pairs of contrasting traits
slides.body_md: In each pair, one form appeared in all the F1 plants: the **dominant** trait.

visual.alt: Table of the seven pea characters with their dominant and recessive forms

slides.narration: Here are the seven characters. Notice something tricky: for pod colour, green is dominant, but for seed colour, yellow is dominant. Learn each pair separately, because examiners like to test exactly this kind of detail.

slides.heading: A monohybrid cross
slides.body_md: Mendel crossed true-breeding **tall** and **dwarf** plants (parental, **P**, generation). All the **F1** plants were tall. When F1 plants self-pollinated, the **F2** had tall and dwarf plants in the ratio **3 : 1**; the dwarf trait had not been lost.

visual.alt: Flow of a monohybrid cross from tall and dwarf parents to an all-tall F1 and an F2 of three tall to one dwarf

slides.narration: This was Mendel’s key observation. The dwarf trait disappeared in the first generation but came back, unchanged, in a quarter of the second generation. So something controlling dwarfness must have been passed on, hidden, through the tall first-generation plants. Mendel called these units factors; today we call them genes.

slides.heading: The Punnett square
slides.body_md: A **Punnett square** shows all the ways gametes can combine. Each F1 plant (Tt) makes **two kinds of gametes, T and t, in equal numbers**. Random fusion gives **TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1** (genotypes) and **3 tall : 1 dwarf** (phenotypes).

slides.narration: Write the gametes of one parent along the top and of the other down the side, then fill each box with the combination. Three boxes contain at least one tall allele, so three quarters of the plants are tall. One box has only dwarf alleles. The square was devised by the geneticist Reginald Punnett.

slides.heading: The language of genetics
slides.body_md: Each character is controlled by a **gene**; its alternative forms are **alleles**. A diploid plant carries **two alleles** for each gene.

visual.alt: Table of genetic terms with meanings and examples

slides.narration: A gene is the unit of inheritance, and alleles are its different forms. If both alleles are the same, the plant is homozygous; if different, heterozygous. The genotype is what the plant carries; the phenotype is what you see. Two plants can share a phenotype, tall, while having different genotypes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: predicting an F2
slides.body_md: An F1 tall pea plant (Tt) is self-pollinated and produces 840 plants. How many are expected to be tall and dwarf? How many of the tall plants are expected to be homozygous?
bullets: Step 1 — Phenotypes: tall $= \dfrac{3}{4} \times 840 = 630$; dwarf $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 840 = 210$.
Step 2 — Genotypes: TT $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 840 = 210$; Tt $= \dfrac{2}{4} \times 840 = 420$.
Step 3 — Of the 630 tall plants, 210 are homozygous, that is $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of them.

visual.alt: Worked table: 630 tall and 210 dwarf; 210 homozygous tall and 420 heterozygous tall

slides.narration: Multiply each fraction by the total. Three quarters of eight hundred and forty is six hundred and thirty tall plants; one quarter is two hundred and ten dwarf. Among the tall plants, only one in three is homozygous, two hundred and ten, while four hundred and twenty are heterozygous. Real counts will be close to these, not exact.

slides.heading: Quick check: F2 genotypes
slides.body_md: What is the genotypic ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the boxes in the Punnett square by genotype, not by appearance.

slides.heading: The test cross
slides.body_md: A tall plant may be TT or Tt. To find out, cross it with a **homozygous recessive** (dwarf, tt) plant: a **test cross**.

visual.alt: Table of test cross outcomes: all tall means homozygous, one tall to one dwarf means heterozygous

slides.narration: The recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles, so it cannot hide anything. Whatever the offspring look like reveals the gametes of the unknown parent. All tall offspring means the plant made only tall gametes; half dwarf offspring means it was heterozygous.

slides.heading: Laws of dominance and segregation
slides.body_md: From his monohybrid crosses, Mendel proposed two principles.

rows: Characters are controlled by discrete units (factors) that occur in pairs; in a dissimilar pair, one member (dominant) is expressed and the other (recessive) is not
The two alleles of a pair do not blend; they separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one of the two

visual.alt: Table of the law of dominance and the law of segregation in brief

slides.narration: The law of dominance explains why the first generation looks like only one parent, and why the three to one ratio appears. The law of segregation explains why the hidden allele comes back unchanged: the two alleles never mix; they separate into different gametes. That is why gametes are said to be pure for a character.

slides.heading: A dihybrid cross
slides.body_md: Mendel then followed **two characters together**: seed shape (round R, wrinkled r) and seed colour (yellow Y, green y). True-breeding round yellow (RRYY) × wrinkled green (rryy) gave an F1 of round yellow (RrYy).

nodes.label: F1 gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry in equal numbers

visual.alt: Flow of a dihybrid cross from round yellow and wrinkled green parents to an F2 ratio of nine to three to three to one

slides.narration: The first generation showed both dominant traits. When these plants self-pollinated, Mendel found four kinds of seeds: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green. Two of these combinations were new, not seen in either original parent. The key is that each plant made four kinds of gametes in equal numbers.

slides.heading: The dihybrid Punnett square
slides.body_md: Sixteen equally likely combinations give **round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1**.

visual.alt: Punnett square of sixteen boxes for a dihybrid cross between two plants heterozygous for seed shape and seed colour

slides.narration: Each parent makes four kinds of gametes, so the square has sixteen boxes. Colour each box by the seed it gives. Nine boxes have at least one round and one yellow allele. Three are round green, three wrinkled yellow, and just one box is wrinkled green. Notice that each character alone still follows three to one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting a dihybrid F2
slides.body_md: An F1 dihybrid (RrYy) is self-pollinated and gives 1600 seeds. How many seeds of each phenotype are expected, and how many are expected to be pure-breeding round yellow (RRYY)?
bullets: Step 1 — Round yellow $= \dfrac{9}{16} \times 1600 = 900$; round green $= \dfrac{3}{16} \times 1600 = 300$.
Step 2 — Wrinkled yellow $= \dfrac{3}{16} \times 1600 = 300$; wrinkled green $= \dfrac{1}{16} \times 1600 = 100$.
Step 3 — RRYY is one box in sixteen: $\dfrac{1}{16} \times 1600 = 100$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 900, 300, 300 and 100 seeds, with 100 pure-breeding round yellow

slides.narration: One sixteenth of sixteen hundred is one hundred, which makes the arithmetic easy. Round yellow is nine sixteenths, nine hundred; each one-recessive class is three sixteenths, three hundred; wrinkled green is one hundred. Of the nine hundred round yellow seeds, only one hundred will breed true for both characters.

slides.heading: Law of independent assortment
slides.body_md: **When two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair is independent of the other.** The dihybrid ratio is the product of two monohybrid ratios: (3 : 1) × (3 : 1) = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

visual.alt: Table showing the dihybrid fractions as products of the monohybrid fractions

slides.narration: Independent assortment means the gene for seed shape does not care which seed colour allele it travels with. So you can multiply probabilities: three quarters round times three quarters yellow gives nine sixteenths. This multiplication trick is the fastest way to solve dihybrid problems without drawing all sixteen boxes.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Mendel (1856–1863): garden pea, 14 true-breeding varieties, 7 pairs of contrasting traits, large samples and statistics.
Monohybrid F2: phenotypes 3 : 1, genotypes 1 : 2 : 1 (TT : Tt : tt).
Test cross with the homozygous recessive: all dominant → homozygous; 1 : 1 → heterozygous.
Dihybrid F2: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; dihybrid test cross: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.
Laws: dominance; segregation (alleles separate into gametes); independent assortment (pairs segregate independently).

visual.alt: Summary table of the four key Mendelian ratios

slides.narration: To recap: Mendel’s careful counting revealed that characters are carried by paired factors that separate into gametes and combine at random. Learn the four key ratios: three to one, one to one, nine to three to three to one, and one to one to one to one. In Part 2 we will see when these ratios change, and why.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always show **gametes** before the Punnett square, and write both **genotypic and phenotypic** ratios.
Use **standard symbols**: capital letter for dominant, same small letter for recessive.
In probability questions, **multiply** independent fractions (3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16).
Remember: pod colour **green** is dominant; seed colour **yellow** is dominant.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Show the gametes every time; most lost marks come from skipping them. Give both ratios. Use the same letter for both alleles of a gene. Multiply fractions for independent genes. And watch the pea colour trap: green pods, but yellow seeds, are dominant.

goals: Explain incomplete dominance, co-dominance and multiple alleles with examples
State the chromosomal theory of inheritance
Explain linkage and recombination from Morgan’s experiments

slides.heading: Beyond Mendel
slides.body_md: Part 2 — patterns that do not follow the simple 3 : 1, and how genes on chromosomes explain them.

visual.alt: Flow of topics in Part 2 from incomplete dominance to linkage

slides.narration: Mendel’s rules are the foundation, but nature has many variations on them. In this part we meet traits where neither allele dominates, genes with more than two alleles, one gene affecting many traits, and many genes affecting one trait. Then we see how genes sit on chromosomes, which explains why some genes travel together.

slides.heading: Incomplete dominance
slides.body_md: In the snapdragon (Antirrhinum), true-breeding **red** (RR) × **white** (rr) gives a **pink** F1 (Rr): neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote is **intermediate**.

visual.alt: Flow of incomplete dominance in snapdragon from red and white parents to pink F1 and an F2 of one red to two pink to one white

slides.narration: Pink snapdragons might look like blending, but they are not. When the pink plants are crossed, red and white flowers reappear unchanged in the next generation. The alleles stayed separate; only their effect in the heterozygote was intermediate. Mendel’s law of segregation still holds.

slides.heading: Snapdragon F2
slides.body_md: With incomplete dominance the **phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio: 1 : 2 : 1**, because each genotype has its own phenotype.

slides.narration: In this square, each genotype produces a different colour: two red alleles give red, one of each gives pink, and two white alleles give white. So the phenotype ratio is the same as the genotype ratio, one to two to one, instead of three to one.

slides.heading: What dominance really means
slides.body_md: A gene carries information to make a product, often an **enzyme**. A changed allele may make a **normal**, a **less efficient** or a **non-functional** enzyme, or **none**.

rows: A normal or equally effective enzyme
A product with an intermediate effect

visual.alt: Table showing how the product of a modified allele decides whether it behaves as equivalent, recessive or incompletely dominant

slides.narration: Dominance is not a fight between alleles. Think of an enzyme. If one normal allele makes enough enzyme for the full effect, a broken allele beside it goes unnoticed, so it behaves as recessive. If one normal allele makes only half the product and half is not enough, the heterozygote looks intermediate.

slides.heading: Co-dominance and multiple alleles: ABO blood groups
slides.body_md: The **ABO** blood groups are controlled by gene **I** with three alleles: **Iᴬ**, **Iᴮ** and **i**. Iᴬ and Iᴮ make different sugars on red blood cells; i makes none. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are **co-dominant**; both are dominant over i. Three alleles give **six genotypes** and **four** blood groups.

visual.alt: Table of six ABO genotypes and the four blood groups they give

slides.narration: Blood group AB shows co-dominance: both alleles are fully expressed and the cells carry both kinds of sugar. The gene also shows multiple alleles, three in the population, although each person carries only two. That is why there are six possible genotypes but only four blood groups.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: blood groups of the children
slides.body_md: A father of blood group A (Iᴬi) and a mother of blood group B (Iᴮi) have children. Which blood groups are possible, and with what probability each?
bullets: Step 1 — Gametes: father Iᴬ or i; mother Iᴮ or i, each half.
Step 2 — Combinations: IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O).
Conclusion — all four blood groups are possible in one family.

visual.alt: Worked Punnett table: children can be AB, A, B or O, each with probability one quarter

slides.narration: Because both parents are heterozygous, each can pass on the hidden allele for group O. The four combinations are equally likely, so a child has a one in four chance of each blood group: A, B, AB or O. This surprises many families, but it is exactly what the alleles predict.

slides.heading: Quick check: ABO genotypes
slides.body_md: How many different genotypes are possible for the human ABO blood groups?
slides.narration: Quick check. Three alleles, two at a time, including identical pairs.

slides.heading: Pleiotropy
slides.body_md: A single gene can affect **more than one** phenotype: **pleiotropy**. The underlying cause is usually the gene’s effect on a metabolic pathway.

rows: A mutation in the gene for the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation
BB: large starch grains, round seeds; bb: small grains, wrinkled seeds; Bb: round seeds but intermediate grain size

visual.alt: Table of two examples of pleiotropy

slides.narration: Pea seed shape is a lovely example. One gene controls starch synthesis. For seed shape, the round allele is dominant. But if you look at starch grain size, the heterozygote is intermediate. So dominance is not a property of the gene itself; it depends on which phenotype you look at.

slides.heading: Polygenic inheritance
slides.body_md: Traits such as **human skin colour** and height are controlled by **three or more genes**, each adding a small effect, and are influenced by the **environment**. They show a **continuous** range rather than distinct classes.

visual.alt: Table of a three-gene model of skin colour: six, three or zero pigment alleles give darkest, intermediate or lightest

slides.narration: In a simple model of skin colour, three genes each have an allele that adds pigment. A person with six such alleles has the darkest skin, with none the lightest, and with three an intermediate shade. Because many combinations give each total, and because sunlight and nutrition also matter, we see a smooth range of skin colours.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how many classes?
slides.body_md: Using the three-gene model, two parents are both heterozygous for all three genes (AaBbCc). How many skin-colour classes are possible among their children, and what fraction will have the darkest skin?
bullets: Step 1 — Each child can carry 0 to 6 pigment alleles: $2 \times 3 + 1 = 7$ classes.
Step 2 — Darkest needs AA, BB and CC; each has probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$.
Step 3 — Independent genes: $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{64} \approx 0.0156$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 7 classes from zero to six pigment alleles; the darkest class is one sixty-fourth

slides.narration: Count the possible totals of pigment alleles, from zero to six. That is seven classes. To be in the darkest class, a child must get the pigment allele from both parents for all three genes. Each gene gives a one in four chance, and multiplying three of them gives one in sixty-four. The middle classes are the most common.

slides.heading: Quick check: polygenic traits
slides.body_md: Which feature is typical of a polygenic trait?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about how human height varies across a class.

slides.heading: The chromosomal theory of inheritance
slides.body_md: Mendel’s work was **rediscovered in 1900** by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak. **Sutton and Boveri** noticed that chromosomes behave like Mendel’s factors and proposed the **chromosomal theory of inheritance**: genes are located on chromosomes.

rows: Segregate at gamete formation; one of each pair per gamete
One pair separates independently of another

visual.alt: Table of the parallel behaviour of genes and chromosomes

slides.narration: When microscopes improved, biologists could watch chromosomes during meiosis. Sutton and Boveri saw that chromosomes come in pairs, separate into gametes and sort independently, just like Mendel’s factors. They concluded that genes must be carried on chromosomes. This united genetics with the study of cells.

slides.heading: Morgan and the fruit fly
slides.body_md: **Thomas Hunt Morgan** gave experimental proof using the fruit fly **Drosophila melanogaster**.

rows: Grows on a simple synthetic medium
Life cycle of about two weeks
Clear differences between male and female
Many heritable variations visible under low magnification

visual.alt: Table of reasons why Drosophila is suitable for genetic experiments

slides.narration: Morgan needed an organism that bred fast and showed many visible variations. The fruit fly was perfect: cheap to raise on simple food, a new generation every two weeks or so, hundreds of offspring from one mating, and easily seen differences in eye colour, body colour and wing size.

slides.heading: Linkage and recombination
slides.body_md: Morgan found that some genes on the **same chromosome** (here, X-linked genes) did not assort independently: parental combinations were far more common than new ones. **Linkage** is the physical association of genes on a chromosome; **recombination** is the generation of non-parental combinations.

slides.narration: Genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together because they travel as one piece. But during meiosis, homologous chromosomes can swap segments by crossing over. Genes close together are rarely separated by a crossover; genes far apart are separated often. So the amount of recombination tells us how far apart genes are.

slides.heading: Measuring linkage
slides.body_md: Morgan crossed flies differing in linked genes and counted the recombinants.

rows: Body colour and eye colour (yellow and white)
Eye colour and wing size (white and miniature)

visual.alt: Table of two gene pairs in Drosophila with their recombination frequencies and interpretation

slides.narration: For two genes affecting body colour and eye colour, only about one percent of offspring were recombinants, so these genes are very close together. For eye colour and wing size, more than a third were recombinants, so they are far apart. Morgan’s student Alfred Sturtevant used such frequencies to draw the first maps of gene positions on a chromosome.

slides.heading: Quick check: linkage
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about two genes with 1.3 percent recombination.
slides.narration: Quick check. Low recombination tells you what about the distance between genes?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Incomplete dominance: snapdragon red × white → pink; F2 1 : 2 : 1 (phenotype = genotype).
Co-dominance + multiple alleles: ABO (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i): six genotypes, four blood groups.
Pleiotropy: one gene, many effects (phenylketonuria; pea starch gene). Polygenic: many genes, one trait, continuous variation (skin colour).
Chromosomal theory (Sutton and Boveri): genes on chromosomes; proof by Morgan with Drosophila.
Linkage: genes on one chromosome travel together; recombination frequency reflects distance (yellow–white 1.3%, white–miniature 37.2%); gene maps by Sturtevant.

visual.alt: Summary table of inheritance patterns and their key results

slides.narration: To recap: dominance can be complete, incomplete or shared. One gene can have many alleles, or many effects. Many genes can shape one trait. And genes sit on chromosomes, so linked genes tend to stay together, with crossing over occasionally separating them in proportion to their distance apart.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For incomplete dominance, say **why** it is not blending: parental types reappear in F2.
Write ABO genotypes with **Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i** and state **six genotypes, four phenotypes**.
Distinguish **pleiotropy** (one gene, many traits) from **polygenic** (many genes, one trait).
Low recombination = **tight linkage** = genes **close together**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Explain that incomplete dominance is not blending. Use the correct allele symbols for blood groups. Never confuse pleiotropy with polygenic inheritance; the words are opposites. And link low recombination with genes that are close together on a chromosome.

slides.heading: Sex determination and genetic disorders
slides.body_md: Part 3 — how chromosomes decide sex, and how changes in genes and chromosomes cause disorders.

visual.alt: Flow from sex chromosomes to sex determination, sex-linked traits, pedigrees and disorders

slides.narration: In this part we look at a special pair of chromosomes, the sex chromosomes. They decide whether an individual is male or female, and genes on them show unusual patterns of inheritance. We will also learn how to read family trees and meet some important genetic disorders.

slides.heading: Mechanisms of sex determination
slides.body_md: **Henking** (1891) traced a nuclear structure in insect sperm, the **X body**; it was later named the X chromosome. Sex chromosomes differ from **autosomes**.

visual.alt: Table of XO, XY and ZW sex-determination systems with examples and the heterogametic sex

slides.narration: In grasshoppers, males have just one X chromosome, so half their sperm carry an X and half carry none. In humans and fruit flies, males have one X and one Y chromosome. In both cases the male is heterogametic, making two kinds of gametes. Birds are the opposite: the female makes two kinds of eggs, so the female decides the sex of the chick.

slides.heading: Sex determination in humans
slides.body_md: Humans have **22 pairs of autosomes** and **one pair of sex chromosomes**. Every ovum carries **X**; sperms carry **X or Y** in equal numbers. So **the sperm decides the sex**, and every pregnancy has an even chance of a girl or a boy.

slides.narration: This square should end a common myth. The mother contributes an X chromosome every time. The father’s sperm carries either an X or a Y. If an X-carrying sperm fertilises the egg, the child is a girl; if a Y-carrying sperm does, a boy. It is a matter of chance, decided by the sperm.

slides.heading: Honey bees: haplodiploidy
slides.body_md: In honey bees, sex depends on the **number of chromosome sets**. Fertilised eggs (32 chromosomes) become **females** — the queen or workers. **Unfertilised** eggs develop by **parthenogenesis** into **males (drones)** with 16 chromosomes.

visual.alt: Flow of haplodiploid sex determination in honey bees

slides.narration: Honey bees break the X and Y pattern completely. A drone develops from an unfertilised egg, so it has only one set of chromosomes and no father, though it can have a grandfather. Since a drone is already haploid, it makes sperm by mitosis, not meiosis. This system is called haplodiploid.

slides.body_md: In birds, which parent decides the sex of the offspring, and why?

slides.narration: In a pedigree, squares are males and circles are females. A filled shape means the person shows the trait; a circle with a dot is a carrier female. A horizontal line joins parents, and a vertical line drops down to their children, with generations numbered in Roman numerals. The example follows a recessive trait carried on the X chromosome.

slides.heading: Sex-linked inheritance: haemophilia and colour blindness
slides.body_md: Both are caused by **recessive alleles on the X chromosome**. A male has only one X, so a single recessive allele shows; a female needs two. So these disorders are **much commoner in males**, and the allele passes from a **carrier mother to her sons**.

rows: A protein in the blood-clotting chain is affected; a small cut may bleed for a long time
Affected females are very rare (mother at least a carrier and father affected); seen in the family of Queen Victoria
Defect in red or green cone cells of the eye; cannot tell red from green
About 8 percent of males and 0.4 percent of females

visual.alt: Table of haemophilia and colour blindness with the defect and notes

slides.narration: Why do these disorders mostly affect boys? A boy gets his only X chromosome from his mother. If that X carries the faulty allele, he has no second X to cover it. A girl must inherit faulty alleles from both parents to be affected, which is much rarer. Carrier women are usually healthy but can pass the allele on.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a carrier mother
slides.body_md: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia marries a man with normal blood clotting. What are the chances for their children?
bullets: Step 1 — Mother: one normal X and one X carrying the allele; father: normal X and Y.
Step 2 — Daughters (get father’s normal X): normal 1/4 of all children, carrier 1/4, affected 0.
Step 3 — Sons (get father’s Y): normal 1/4, affected 1/4 of all children.
Conclusion — each son has a 1 in 2 chance of haemophilia; no daughter is affected, but half the daughters are carriers.

visual.alt: Worked table: carrier mother and normal father give normal and carrier daughters and normal and affected sons, each one quarter; no affected daughters

slides.narration: All daughters receive the father’s normal X, so none can be affected, but half receive the mother’s faulty X and become carriers. All sons receive the father’s Y and one of the mother’s two X chromosomes, so half the sons are affected. Among all the children, each of these four outcomes has a one in four chance.

slides.heading: Quick check: from whom?
slides.body_md: A boy has haemophilia, but both his parents have normal blood clotting. From whom did he inherit the allele?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which parent gave the boy his X chromosome?

slides.heading: Autosomal Mendelian disorders
slides.body_md: Mendelian disorders are caused by alteration or mutation in a **single gene**; they may be dominant or recessive, autosomal or sex-linked.

rows: Glutamic acid replaced by valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain (codon GAG → GUG); red cells become sickle-shaped at low oxygen
Lack of the enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine; phenylalanine builds up and damages the brain
Too little globin made (α: genes HBA1, HBA2 on chromosome 16; β: gene HBB on chromosome 11); anaemia

visual.alt: Table of three autosomal recessive disorders with cause and effect

slides.narration: Sickle-cell anaemia comes from a single change of one base in the gene for beta globin, which swaps one amino acid. The changed haemoglobin makes red cells bend into sickle shapes when oxygen is low. Thalassemia differs: the globin itself is normal but too little is made. So sickle-cell is a problem of quality, and thalassemia a problem of quantity.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two carriers of sickle-cell trait
slides.body_md: Both parents are healthy carriers of the sickle-cell allele (HbᴬHbˢ). What are the chances that a child is affected, a carrier, or unaffected?
bullets: Step 1 — Each parent gives Hbᴬ or Hbˢ with probability 1/2.
Step 2 — HbᴬHbᴬ (unaffected) 0.25; HbᴬHbˢ (carrier) 0.5; HbˢHbˢ (affected) 0.25.
Conclusion — 1 in 4 affected, 1 in 2 carriers, 1 in 4 unaffected, in every pregnancy.

visual.alt: Worked Punnett table: one quarter unaffected, one half carriers, one quarter affected

slides.narration: This is a monohybrid cross with a recessive disorder. Each parent passes on either the normal or the sickle allele, equally likely. One quarter of children inherit two sickle alleles and have the disease; half are healthy carriers like their parents; one quarter inherit two normal alleles. Genetic counselling helps families understand these chances.

slides.heading: Chromosomal disorders
slides.body_md: Caused by **absence, excess or abnormal arrangement** of chromosomes. Failure of chromatids to separate in cell division (non-disjunction) causes **aneuploidy** (gain or loss of a chromosome); failure of cytokinesis after telophase gives **polyploidy**, often seen in plants.

rows: Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partly open mouth, broad palm with a characteristic crease; delayed physical, psychomotor and mental development
Male development with some feminine features (gynaecomastia); sterile
Female; sterile, ovaries rudimentary; lack of secondary sexual characters

visual.alt: Table of Down’s, Klinefelter’s and Turner’s syndromes with karyotype and main features

slides.narration: An extra copy of chromosome twenty-one causes Down’s syndrome, first described by Langdon Down in eighteen sixty-six. An extra X in a male causes Klinefelter’s syndrome, and a missing X in a female causes Turner’s syndrome. People with these conditions deserve care and respect; early support helps them live fuller lives.

slides.heading: Quick check: chromosome numbers
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about Turner’s syndrome.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the chromosomes in each condition carefully.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: XO (grasshopper) and XY (humans, Drosophila): male heterogametic; ZW (birds): female heterogametic; honey bee: fertilised eggs → females (32), unfertilised → drones (16).
Human sex is decided by the sperm; each pregnancy 1 : 1.
Pedigree symbols: square male, circle female, filled affected, dot carrier.
X-linked recessive: haemophilia, colour blindness; commoner in males; carrier mother → half her sons affected.
Autosomal recessive: sickle-cell anaemia (Glu → Val, GAG → GUG), phenylketonuria, thalassemia (α on 16, β on 11).
Chromosomal: Down’s (trisomy 21), Klinefelter’s (47, XXY), Turner’s (45, XO).

visual.alt: Summary table of disorders by category

slides.narration: To recap: sex is decided by different systems in different animals, and in humans by the father’s sperm. Pedigrees let us follow traits through families. X-linked recessive disorders mostly affect males. Sickle-cell anaemia, phenylketonuria and thalassemia are autosomal recessive. And extra or missing chromosomes cause Down’s, Klinefelter’s and Turner’s syndromes.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In pedigree questions, first ask: **are mostly males affected?** If yes, suspect X-linked recessive.
For sickle-cell anaemia, give the **amino acid change** and the **codon change**.
Write karyotypes exactly: **47, XXY** and **45, XO**; Down’s is **trisomy 21**.
Contrast **sickle-cell** (wrong globin) with **thalassemia** (too little globin).
slides.narration: Exam tips. When reading a pedigree, check who is affected: mostly males suggests an X-linked recessive trait. For sickle-cell anaemia, give both the amino acid change and the codon change. Write chromosome numbers exactly for the syndromes. And contrast sickle-cell anaemia with thalassemia: quality versus quantity.

notes.title: Principles of Inheritance and Variation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Mendel’s experiments and the monohybrid cross
sections.body_md:
**Inheritance** is the process by which characters pass from parent to progeny; **variation** is the degree to which progeny differ from their parents. **Gregor Mendel** crossed garden peas for seven years (1856–1863), used **14 true-breeding varieties** (seven pairs of contrasting traits) and applied statistics to large samples.

| Character | Dominant | Recessive |
|---|---|---|
| Stem height | Tall | Dwarf |
| Flower colour | Violet | White |
| Flower position | Axial | Terminal |
| Pod shape | Inflated | Constricted |
| Pod colour | Green | Yellow |
| Seed shape | Round | Wrinkled |
| Seed colour | Yellow | Green |

**Monohybrid cross:** tall (TT) × dwarf (tt) → F1 all tall (Tt) → F1 selfed → F2 **3 tall : 1 dwarf**; genotypes **TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1**. A **gene** has alternative forms, **alleles**; homozygous (TT, tt), heterozygous (Tt); genotype vs phenotype. The **Punnett square** (Reginald Punnett) shows all gamete combinations.

**Test cross:** a dominant-phenotype organism × the **homozygous recessive**: all dominant offspring → homozygous; 1 : 1 → heterozygous.

**Law of dominance:** characters are controlled by discrete paired units (factors); in a dissimilar pair one (dominant) is expressed. **Law of segregation:** alleles do not blend; the two members of a pair separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets only one.

key_terms.definition_md: An alternative form of a gene.
Cross of an organism showing the dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive, to find its genotype.
The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one.

sections.heading: 2. Dihybrid cross and independent assortment
sections.body_md:
Round yellow (RRYY) × wrinkled green (rryy) → F1 round yellow (RrYy). F1 gametes: **RY, Ry, rY, ry** in equal numbers. F2: **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**.

**Law of independent assortment:** when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair is independent of the other. Hence 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 = (3 : 1) × (3 : 1), and probabilities of independent genes **multiply**.

Dihybrid **test cross** (RrYy × rryy) → **1 : 1 : 1 : 1**.

Mendel published in 1865; the work was rediscovered in **1900** by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak.

sections.heading: 3. Deviations from Mendelian ratios
sections.body_md:
**Incomplete dominance:** snapdragon (Antirrhinum) red (RR) × white (rr) → pink F1 (Rr); F2 **1 red : 2 pink : 1 white** (phenotypic = genotypic ratio). Alleles still segregate; this is not blending.

**What dominance means:** a gene makes a product (often an enzyme). A modified allele may make a normal, a less efficient or a non-functional enzyme, or none. If the unmodified allele alone gives the full phenotype, the modified allele behaves as **recessive**.

**Co-dominance and multiple alleles:** ABO blood groups — gene **I**, alleles **Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i**; Iᴬ and Iᴮ are co-dominant, both dominant over i.
| Genotypes | Blood group |
|---|---|
| IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi | A |
| IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi | B |
| IᴬIᴮ | AB |
| ii | O |
Six genotypes, four phenotypes. Multiple alleles are found only in a population; an individual has two.

**Pleiotropy:** one gene, many effects — phenylketonuria (mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation); pea starch gene (BB large starch grains and round seeds; bb small grains, wrinkled; Bb round seeds but intermediate grains — dominance depends on the phenotype studied).

**Polygenic inheritance:** traits controlled by three or more genes with additive effects and environmental influence, giving continuous variation — human skin colour (AABBCC darkest, aabbcc lightest, AaBbCc intermediate) and height.

key_terms.definition_md: Heterozygote shows a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes.
Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote, as in blood group AB.
A single gene affecting more than one phenotype.
A trait controlled by several genes, showing continuous variation.

sections.heading: 4. Chromosomal theory, linkage and recombination
sections.body_md:
**Sutton and Boveri** noted that chromosomes, like Mendel's factors, occur in pairs, segregate at gamete formation and assort independently, and proposed the **chromosomal theory of inheritance**. **T. H. Morgan** proved it with **Drosophila melanogaster** (simple synthetic medium, life cycle of about two weeks, many progeny per mating, clear sex differences, many visible variations).

Morgan's dihybrid crosses with **X-linked genes** gave far more parental than recombinant types. **Linkage:** physical association of genes on a chromosome. **Recombination:** generation of non-parental gene combinations (by crossing over).
- Body colour and eye colour (yellow, white): **1.3 percent** recombination — tightly linked.
- Eye colour and wing size (white, miniature): **37.2 percent** — loosely linked.

Tightly linked genes show low recombination; loosely linked genes show high recombination. **Sturtevant** used recombination frequency as a measure of distance to **map gene positions** on chromosomes.

key_terms.definition_md: Physical association of two or more genes on a chromosome, so they tend to be inherited together.
Generation of non-parental gene combinations, through crossing over.

sections.heading: 5. Sex determination
sections.body_md:
**Henking** (1891) named the **X body** in insect sperm (later the X chromosome).
| System | Example | Female | Male |
|---|---|---|---|
| XO | Grasshopper | XX | XO |
| XY | Humans, Drosophila | XX | XY |
| ZW | Birds | ZW | ZZ |

XO and XY: **male heterogamety**; ZW: **female heterogamety**. Humans: 22 pairs of autosomes + XX or XY; ova all carry X; sperms carry X or Y (50 : 50), so the **sperm decides the sex**.

**Honey bee (haplodiploidy):** fertilised eggs (32 chromosomes) → females (queen, workers); unfertilised eggs → males (drones, 16 chromosomes) by **parthenogenesis**. Drones make sperm by **mitosis**, have no father and so no sons, but have a grandfather and can have grandsons.

key_terms.definition_md: Chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes.
The male produces two kinds of gametes with respect to sex chromosomes.
Sex determination in which males develop from unfertilised (haploid) eggs and females from fertilised (diploid) eggs.

sections.heading: 6. Pedigree analysis and sex-linked disorders
sections.body_md:
A **pedigree** follows a trait over generations of a family; standard symbols: square (male), circle (female), filled (affected), dot in circle (carrier female), horizontal line (mating), double line (consanguineous mating), Roman numerals for generations.

**X-linked recessive disorders** (allele on the X chromosome; males hemizygous):
- **Haemophilia:** a protein in the clotting cascade is affected; a simple cut may bleed non-stop. Transmitted from unaffected carrier females to some sons; affected females are very rare (mother at least a carrier and father haemophilic). Seen in the descendants of Queen Victoria.
- **Colour blindness:** defect in red or green cone cells; about 8 percent of males and 0.4 percent of females; a daughter is colour blind only if her mother is at least a carrier and her father is colour blind.

Carrier mother × normal father → each son 1/2 chance affected; no daughter affected; half of daughters carriers. Affected father × normal mother → all daughters carriers, no son affected.

A heterozygous individual who carries a recessive allele without showing the trait.

sections.heading: 7. Mendelian and chromosomal disorders
sections.body_md:
**Mendelian disorders** (single-gene): haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia.
- **Sickle-cell anaemia** (autosomal recessive): **glutamic acid (Glu) replaced by valine (Val)** at the **sixth** position of the **β-globin** chain, from the single base change **GAG → GUG**. Disease only in **HbˢHbˢ**; **HbᴬHbˢ** are carriers. The changed haemoglobin polymerises at low oxygen, so red cells become sickle-shaped.
- **Phenylketonuria** (autosomal recessive): the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine is missing; phenylalanine and its derivatives build up and damage the brain (mental retardation) and are excreted in urine.
- **Thalassemia** (autosomal recessive): reduced synthesis of a globin chain, causing anaemia. **α**: genes **HBA1, HBA2** on **chromosome 16**; **β**: gene **HBB** on **chromosome 11**. Thalassemia is a **quantitative** problem (too little globin); sickle-cell is **qualitative** (wrong globin).

**Chromosomal disorders:** non-disjunction gives **aneuploidy**; failure of cytokinesis gives **polyploidy** (common in plants).
| Syndrome | Karyotype | Features |
|---|---|---|
| Down's | Trisomy 21 | Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partly open mouth, broad palm with a characteristic crease; delayed physical, psychomotor and mental development |
| Klinefelter's | 47, XXY | Overall masculine development with feminine features such as gynaecomastia; sterile |
| Turner's | 45, XO | Sterile female, rudimentary ovaries, lack of secondary sexual characters |

key_terms.definition_md: Gain or loss of one or more chromosomes, caused by failure of chromatids to separate.
Presence of an extra copy of a chromosome, as chromosome 21 in Down’s syndrome.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Skipping gametes in crosses, or giving only one of the genotypic and phenotypic ratios.
- Writing that the F1 of incomplete dominance shows "blending" (alleles still segregate).
- Confusing pleiotropy with polygenic inheritance.
- Saying ABO has four genotypes (there are six).
- Saying birds have male heterogamety (it is female: ZW).
- Writing sickle-cell as "Val replaced by Glu" (it is Glu → Val, GAG → GUG).
- Mixing up karyotypes: Klinefelter's 47, XXY; Turner's 45, XO.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: ratio, term, example or karyotype.
- 2–3-mark answers: correct cross with gametes (1–2) + ratio and conclusion (1).
- 5-mark answers: a full cross (P, gametes, F1, F2 with Punnett square) with ratios (3) + the law it illustrates (1) + one more point (1).
- Case-based items: reading a pedigree or a set of offspring counts, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Define linkage and recombination. Why did Morgan’s dihybrid crosses with X-linked genes not give the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio?

**Linkage** is the physical association of genes on the same chromosome, so they tend to be inherited together. **Recombination** is the generation of non-parental gene combinations, through crossing over.

Mendel’s 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 assumes **independent assortment**. Morgan’s genes were on the **same (X) chromosome**, so they did not assort independently: parental combinations were much more frequent than recombinants, and the ratio deviated.

questions.stem_md: Describe how Morgan’s work with Drosophila supported the chromosomal theory of inheritance and led to the idea of linkage. How are recombination frequencies used to map genes?

answer.model_answer_md:
**Chromosomal theory.** Sutton and Boveri noted that chromosomes, like Mendel’s factors, occur in pairs, segregate during gamete formation and assort independently, and proposed that genes are carried on chromosomes.

**Morgan’s choice.** He used Drosophila because it grows on a simple medium, has a life cycle of about two weeks, produces many offspring and shows many visible heritable variations.

**Linkage.** He made dihybrid crosses with genes on the X chromosome, for example for body colour and eye colour. The F2 did not show 9 : 3 : 3 : 1: parental combinations were far more frequent than new ones. He concluded that genes on the same chromosome are linked and are inherited together, and that new combinations (recombinants) arise by crossing over.

**Mapping.** Tightly linked genes (yellow and white, 1.3 percent) rarely recombine; loosely linked genes (white and miniature, 37.2 percent) often do. Sturtevant used recombination frequency as a measure of the distance between genes to map their positions on a chromosome.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between Mendelian and chromosomal disorders. Describe one autosomal Mendelian disorder and two chromosomal disorders, giving their cause and main features.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Difference.** Mendelian disorders are caused by alteration or mutation in a single gene and follow Mendelian patterns that can be traced in pedigrees. Chromosomal disorders are caused by the absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes.

**Phenylketonuria (autosomal recessive Mendelian).** The enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine is missing, so phenylalanine and its derivatives accumulate and damage the brain, causing mental retardation; they are also excreted in the urine.

answer.model_answer_md:
**The disorder.** β-thalassemia is an autosomal recessive blood disorder. It arises from mutation or deletion of the HBB gene on chromosome 11, which reduces the synthesis of β-globin chains. Too little haemoglobin is made, causing anaemia; this is why it is a quantitative problem, unlike sickle-cell anaemia, in which an incorrect globin is made.

**Risk.** Each carrier passes the faulty allele with probability one half. In every pregnancy, there is a one in four chance of an affected child, a one in two chance of a healthy carrier, and a one in four chance of a child with two normal alleles. The chances are the same for each pregnancy.

**Counselling.** A counsellor would explain these chances clearly, point out that carriers are healthy, discuss prenatal testing options and medical care for affected children, and support the couple’s own informed decision without blame.

**Evaluation.** The risk is real but not certain; knowing their carrier status lets them plan with accurate information.
